title: Make your LLM app a Domain Expert: How to Build an Expert System — Christopher Lovejoy, Anterior

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's central focus is evaluation methodology—failure mode ontologies, user-centric metrics, production-derived eval datasets, and eval-driven iteration for domain-specific AI. The concrete application is clinical reasoning for health insurance administration, grounding the talk in healthcare and enterprise operations. The described system operates in production serving 50 million lives, with continuous evaluation and iteration as core lifecycle activities. Requires familiarity with LLM applications and evaluation concepts but remains accessible to practitioners building vertical AI. A structured conference presentation with slides, dashboard demos, and a Q&A session. Claims are backed by a real production system at Anterior with quantitative results showing accuracy improvement from 95% to 99%.

summary: Christopher Lovejoy introduces himself as a medical doctor (8 years) turned AI engineer (7 years), now at Anterior, a New York-based clinician-led company providing clinical reasoning tools to automate health insurance administration, serving providers covering 50 million American lives. His central thesis: in vertical AI, the system for incorporating domain insights is far more important than model sophistication. Models reason well and reach a strong baseline (~95% accuracy on medical necessity reviews), but reaching near-perfect performance (~99%) requires building systems that give the pipeline domain context and enable rapid iteration with customers. He frames the core challenge as the 'last mile problem'—providing models with context and understanding of specific customer and industry workflows. He illustrates this with a clinical case: a 78-year-old female with knee pain recommended for arthroscopy, where the AI must determine if there was documentation of unsuccessful conservative therapy for at least six weeks, revealing hidden ambiguity around what constitutes conservative therapy, what counts as unsuccessful, and what documentation is required. Lovejoy then introduces Anterior's 'Adaptive Domain Intelligence Engine,' which has two main parts: measurement and improvement. On the measurement side, he describes defining the metrics users truly care about (e.g., minimizing false approvals in health insurance), and designing a failure mode ontology—a structured categorization of how the AI fails, led by domain experts. He shows an internal dashboard where clinicians review AI outputs alongside medical records and guidelines, marking correctness and labeling failure modes. On the improvement side, failure mode datasets derived from production data are given to engineers, who iterate against them and track performance by pipeline version and failure mode. Going further, domain experts are brought into the iteration itself through tooling with a 'domain knowledge addition button' that lets clinicians suggest domain knowledge while reviewing cases—for example, clarifying how to interpret 'suspicion' of a condition or adding a clinical scoring system. This enables same-day fixes: production data flows through, gets analyzed clinically, domain knowledge is added, validated with evals, and deployed. Domain expert reviews thus produce three outputs: performance metrics, failure modes, and suggested improvements. The overall flow is: production app generates AI outputs, domain experts review and generate insights, a domain-expert PM prioritizes and directs engineers to fix specific failure modes to target thresholds, engineers iterate using ready-made failure mode datasets (experimenting with prompting, models, fine-tuning), eval results confirm improvement, and the PM decides whether to go live. Q&A clarifies that domain expert definition depends on the workflow (ideally a doctor for clinical reasoning), bespoke tooling is recommended for tight platform integration, and domain experts can be either in-house hires or customers performing validation. The final takeaway: building a domain-native LLM app requires solving the last mile problem not with more powerful models but with an adaptive domain intelligence engine—a self-improving, data-driven process managed by a domain-expert PM.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Speaker Background and Anterior Overview
sections.summary: Christopher Lovejoy introduces himself as a medical doctor turned AI engineer with 8 years in medicine and 7 years building AI systems. He describes Anterior, a clinician-led company providing clinical reasoning tools for health insurance automation, serving providers covering 50 million American lives. He states his core thesis: the system for incorporating domain insights is more important than model sophistication, and introduces a high-level schematic with a domain-expert PM at the center.

sections.title: The Last Mile Problem
sections.summary: Lovejoy explains why applying LLMs to specialized industries is hard using the 'last mile problem'—the challenge of giving models context about specific workflows. He illustrates with a clinical case: a 78-year-old female with knee pain recommended for arthroscopy, where the AI must determine if there was documentation of unsuccessful conservative therapy for at least six weeks. He unpacks hidden ambiguity in defining conservative therapy, what counts as unsuccessful, and what documentation is required.

sections.title: Measuring Domain-Specific Performance
sections.summary: Lovejoy describes the measurement side of Anterior's Adaptive Domain Intelligence Engine. First, define the metrics users truly care about (e.g., minimizing false approvals in health insurance). Second, design a failure mode ontology—a structured categorization of how the AI fails, led by domain experts. He shows an internal dashboard where clinicians review AI outputs against medical records and guidelines, labeling failures. Combining metric tracking and failure labeling enables prioritization by connecting failure modes to the north-star metric.

sections.title: Improvement via Failure Mode Datasets
sections.summary: Lovejoy describes how production-derived failure mode datasets are given to engineers for iteration. Because they come from production data, they are representative of real input distributions. Engineers iterate against specific failure mode datasets, tracking performance by pipeline version and failure mode, enabling targeted improvements and regression detection across releases.

sections.title: Domain Experts in the Improvement Loop
sections.summary: Lovejoy explains bringing domain experts into the iteration itself through tooling with a 'domain knowledge addition button.' While reviewing cases, clinicians can suggest domain knowledge (e.g., clarifying interpretation of 'suspicion' of a condition or adding a scoring system). Evals validate whether the suggested knowledge improves performance before it goes live, enabling same-day fixes. Domain expert reviews thus produce three outputs: performance metrics, failure modes, and suggested improvements.

sections.title: Q&A: Domain Experts, Tooling, and Users
sections.summary: Lovejoy answers questions: domain expert definition depends on the workflow (ideally a doctor for clinical reasoning, but could be a nurse or junior clinical person for simpler tasks); bespoke tooling is recommended when outputs feed into the broader platform; domain experts can be either in-house hires or customers performing validation, potentially as a customer-facing product.

sections.title: Overall Flow and Final Takeaways
sections.summary: Lovejoy presents the overall flow: production app generates AI outputs, domain experts review and generate insights (metrics, failure modes), a domain-expert PM prioritizes and directs engineers to fix specific failure modes to target thresholds, engineers iterate using ready-made datasets (experimenting with prompting, models, fine-tuning), evals confirm improvement, and the PM decides whether to go live. Final takeaway: solving the last mile problem requires an adaptive domain intelligence engine—a self-improving, data-driven process managed by a domain-expert PM.
